comb-01-c1.text: University of Washington, Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering (CSE 312) (2021). Lecture 1: Intro and Counting Rules (annotated slides, CSE 312 Summer 2021). University of Washington CSE 312.
comb-01-c1.quote: Sum Rule: If you are choosing one thing between 𝑛 options in one group and 𝑚 in another group with no overlap, the total number of options is: 𝑛 + 𝑚.
comb-01-c1.claim: and the two tasks are mutually exclusive (no overlap), then you can do one or the other in m + n ways.

comb-01-c1.text: University of Washington, Paul G. Allen School of Computer Science & Engineering (CSE 312) (2021). Lecture 1: Intro and Counting Rules (annotated slides, CSE 312 Summer 2021). University of Washington CSE 312.
comb-01-c1.quote: Product Rule: If you have a sequential process, where step 𝟏 has 𝒏𝟏 options, step 2 has 𝒏𝟐 options,…,step 𝒌 has 𝒏𝒌 options, and you choose one from each step, the total number of possibilities is 𝒏𝟏 ⋅ 𝒏𝟐 ⋯ 𝒏𝒌
comb-01-c1.claim: if you have to do Task A in m ways AND then Task B in n ways, the total number of combined outcomes is m × n.

comb-01-c3.text: Alex Tsun (Stanford CS109 course notes, from Probability & Statistics with Applications to Computing) (2018). Chapter 1. Combinatorial Theory, 1.1: So You Think You Can Count?. Stanford University CS109 course materials.
comb-01-c3.quote: Informally, to find the number of ways to do something, we could count the number of ways to NOT to do that thing, and subtract it from the total.
comb-01-c3.claim: In set notation, if S is the universal set and A is the set of "bad" outcomes, then the count of "good" outcomes is |S| − |A|.
